metadata.note: Passenger rail at Florence, Alabama and the rest of the Shoals -- Sheffield, Tuscumbia and Muscle Shoals -- from the first locomotive west of the Appalachians to the last streetcar. Four routes and eleven features. East-west through Tuscumbia and Sheffield runs the oldest of them: the Tuscumbia, Courtland and Decatur of 1832, built to carry cotton around the Muscle Shoals rapids, absorbed into the Memphis and Charleston in 1850 and into the Southern Railway in 1894, and carrying the Tennessean until Mar 30 1968. North across the Tennessee River on the Memphis and Charleston's double-decked 1859 bridge lies Florence itself, reached first by that railroad's own branch and from 1888 by the Nashville, Florence and Sheffield -- the L&N -- running 82 miles down from Columbia, Tennessee. South from Tuscumbia the Birmingham, Sheffield and Tennessee River, later the Northern Alabama, ran 95 miles into the Warrior coal field at Parrish. And from 1904 to 1933 the Sheffield Company's electric cars crossed the railroad bridge hourly, having displaced the Southern's own Sheffield-Florence local trains. The features are split by owner as Rule 4 requires, so the same corridor appears more than once with different colours for different eras; the geometry is shared.

metadata.not_yet_sourced: 1. END OF L&N PASSENGER SERVICE, COLUMBIA-FLORENCE-TUSCUMBIA. The single weakest date in this layer. No source consulted names one. The 1948 drawn on ln-columbia-tuscumbia is inferred from the Jul 14 1948 closing of Tuscumbia's 5th Street Station, where these trains terminated. A timetable would settle it. 2. END OF PASSENGER SERVICE, TUSCUMBIA-PARRISH. Drawn to 1948 because Cameron appears in a 1948 company timetable; that is the last positive evidence found, not the last train. 3. CIVIL WAR BREAK ON THE FLORENCE BRIDGE. The bridge was destroyed by Union forces and rebuilt in 1870, but the destruction date is unsourced; 1862 is drawn as an approximation. 4. THE BRIDGE'S OWN DATE. One source says the Memphis and Charleston built it in 1858, another says 1859 with regular trains from Dec 7 1859. Recorded, not resolved; the 1859 date is drawn. 5. THE 1891-1895 SHEFFIELD STREET RAILWAY STEAM DUMMY LINE. Mechanically powered, so it would qualify under Rule 5, but no source gives its route and it is not drawn. 6. THE STREETCAR ROUTE ITSELF. Only the river crossing is sourced. See the geometry_quality note on the two interurban features. 7. HEADWAYS. Every headway_min here is an estimate except the hourly service on the Sheffield Company and Alabama Power features, which is sourced, and the 1936 count of seven trains a day through Lynn on the Northern Alabama feature, which is sourced but counts three companies' trains, not one's. 8. WHETHER THE SOUTHERN'S FLORENCE STOP OUTLASTED 1904. sou-sheffield-florence ends in 1904 because the streetcars are documented to have replaced the local passenger trains that year. Whether any Southern train continued to call at Florence after that has not been checked.
metadata.horsecar_audit: Rule 5 applied at the point of writing rather than retrospectively. Two things were kept off this layer for animal power. The Tuscumbia Railway of 1830 -- 2.1 mi from Tuscumbia down to the Tennessee River landing, and the first railroad chartered or built west of the Appalachians -- is not drawn at all, being horse-worked throughout. The Tuscumbia, Courtland and Decatur is drawn from 1834 and not from the Jun 12 1832 opening of its first two miles, because those first two years were worked by teams of horses over strap rail; 1834 is when the Fulton arrived and the line went over to steam. Both facts are kept in the notes as context, which Rule 5 allows -- what is not allowed is a drawn year that asserts service the horses were providing.
metadata.freight_only_note: Rule 1 applied at the point of writing. Three tempting freight-era extensions were left off. The Old Railroad Bridge carried trains until 1988 and the branch was not abandoned until that September, with the L&N cancelling its operations Apr 10 1986 -- but the passenger trains over it stopped in 1904, so sou-sheffield-florence ends in 1904. The Columbia-Florence line is busy today under the Tennessee Southern Railroad, serving the Port of Florence; it is drawn only to 1948. The Memphis District and the NA / West End District are both live Norfolk Southern freight routes and are drawn only to 1968 and 1948 respectively. All four facts appear in segment notes as context, which is what Rule 1 permits.

segments.note: The first railroad west of the Appalachians, built to carry cotton around the Muscle Shoals rapids that closed the Tennessee River to boats. Incorporated Jan 13 1832; the first two miles, Tuscumbia to Leighton, opened Jun 12 1832. DRAWN FROM 1834, NOT 1832, BECAUSE THE FIRST TWO YEARS WERE HORSE HAULAGE (see Rule 5): the trains were pulled by teams of horses over strap rail until the Fulton -- a 5-ton Edward Bury locomotive built in Liverpool, 8 in cylinders, 16 in stroke, 4 ft 6 in drivers -- was 'first put upon the road about the 1st of June 1834', the first locomotive west of the Appalachians. The line reached Courtland and then Decatur, 44 mi, that same June. Incorporated into the Memphis and Charleston in 1850. The separate 2.1 mi Tuscumbia Railway of 1830, Tuscumbia down to the river landing, is not drawn at all: it was horse-worked throughout its short life. Frequency estimated/unsourced.

segments.note: Chartered 1846 to join the Atlantic coast to the Mississippi, and finished in May 1857, when more than 30,000 people gathered to mark the first railroad connecting the Atlantic to Memphis. Forty miles were in operation by 1853. Between Tuscumbia and Decatur the M&C simply took over the Tuscumbia, Courtland and Decatur's route, which it had absorbed in 1850. The line was fought over hard in the Civil War; no dated service break on this stretch has been sourced, so none is drawn. An 1882 Memphis newspaper advertised through service over it at a $26.25 fare. Became part of the Southern Railway System organised by J. P. Morgan in 1894. Frequency estimated/unsourced.

segments.note: The Tennessean took over as the Washington-Memphis train in 1941, run jointly with the Norfolk and Western, which handled it between Lynchburg and Bristol. It called at Huntsville and in the Shoals on its way to Memphis. Tuscumbia's 5th Street Station saw its last train on Jul 14 1948, ending more than a century of railroad service to the town; the stop moved to a new depot on Shop Pike at 10th Street in Sheffield, which lasted to the end. THE END DATE IS SOURCED: the Tennessean made its final run on Mar 30 1968, ending all Southern Railway passenger service to Memphis and closing Memphis Union Station. Southern was the only railroad serving Alabama that stayed out of Amtrak in 1971, but that only affected its Washington-Atlanta-New Orleans Southern Crescent, not this line, which had already been dark for three years. Frequency estimated/unsourced.

Traced 5.3 mi against about 6 mi documented (Sheffield MP 2 to Florence Union Station MP 8 in the gazetteer). 7.3% of the drawn length is straight-line connector, in three pieces: 163 m where the south approach is no longer mapped, 223 m across the demolished lift span in mid-river, and 236 m where the abandoned north approach converges on the surviving Florence track. segments.note: The branch that first put a passenger train into Florence, over the Memphis and Charleston's double-decked Tennessee River bridge: trains on the upper deck, a public toll wagon road on the lower. The bridge opened to wagons in October 1859 and to regular train service on Dec 7 1859. SOURCE CONFLICT, RECORDED NOT RESOLVED: another account from the same publisher dates the bridge's construction to 1858 and says trains first crossed that year; the December 1859 date is the more specific claim and is the one drawn. THE 1862 END IS AN APPROXIMATION -- Union forces destroyed the bridge during the Civil War, but no date for that has been sourced. Frequency estimated/unsourced.

segments.note: The Southern Railway's Florence branch, three stops long: Sheffield-Muscle Shoals, South Florence, Florence. THE 1904 END IS SOURCED AND IS NOT AN ABANDONMENT -- in 1904 the Sheffield Company's new electric cars replaced the local passenger train service over the bridge, and the streetcars then used the railroad tracks until 1933 (drawn as sheffield-co-shoals-interurban). L&N through trains off the Columbia line kept crossing after 1904. Freight ran over the upper deck until 1988: the L&N cancelled its operations Apr 10 1986, the Southern abandoned what was left of the branch in September 1988, and the bridge came down in 1990, leaving the piers and a restored lower-deck walking trail. None of that is drawn, because none of it carried passengers. Frequency estimated/unsourced.

properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced, 595 points. Traced 87.3 mi against 86.9 mi documented (Columbia 0.0 to Tuscumbia 86.9 in the Tennessee passenger-station gazetteer), 0.4% over. Straight-line connector is 0.4% of the drawn length -- 622 m in three pieces, all of them in the last 7.5 mi across the Tennessee River, and all described under mc-sheffield-florence. The last 7.5 mi are drawn here because that is where these trains actually went: L&N trains off the Columbia line ran through Florence to Sheffield and Tuscumbia over the Memphis and Charleston's bridge under a joint-use agreement dating from 1887, and the daily Nashville train terminated at Tuscumbia. That trackage is therefore drawn twice in this layer -- once here in L&N colours for the L&N's trains, and once as mc-sheffield-florence / sou-sheffield-florence for the bridge owner's own local trains, which stopped in 1904 while the L&N's kept running. LATER ALIGNMENT for the Sheffield to Tuscumbia mile and a half, for the 1916 reason given on the Memphis and Charleston features.

segments.note: Florence's own line north. The Nashville, Florence and Sheffield Railway was formed on May 18 1887 by consolidating the Nashville & Florence and the Tennessee & Alabama; the last 24 mi, St. Joseph to Florence, opened Jul 1 1888, completing an 82-mile main line from Columbia -- 86.9 mi as far as Tuscumbia, which is what is drawn. Reaching Sheffield and Tuscumbia across the Tennessee River meant using the Memphis and Charleston's bridge, which the company obtained joint use of in 1887, so the last 7.5 mi of this feature run over rails it did not own. The L&N held the majority of the stock and operated the road for its owners from Jul 1 1887. Frequency estimated/unsourced.

No source consulted names a date for the end of L&N passenger service on the Columbia-Florence line. The 1948 drawn here is anchored on the only nearby fact available -- the last train out of Tuscumbia's 5th Street Station on Jul 14 1948, 'ending over a century of railroad service to Tuscumbia', Tuscumbia being where these trains terminated. That is an inference, not a citation, and it is the weakest date in this layer. Freight lasted much longer: the L&N cancelled operations over the river bridge on Apr 10 1986, and the Columbia-Florence line is worked today by the Tennessee Southern Railroad, which serves the Port of Florence. segments.note: Florence and Sheffield's line south into the Warrior coal field. Begun in 1884 as the East Tennessee, Virginia and Georgia, renamed the Birmingham and Tennessee River and then the Sheffield and Birmingham in 1885; the track reached Delmar by August 1887 and Delmar to Jasper, 35.32 mi through Lynn, opened May 16 1888. In April 1889 the Sheffield and Birmingham Coal, Iron and Railway Company sold the 87 mi Sheffield-to-Jasper road to Alfred Parrish of Philadelphia, who renamed it the Birmingham, Sheffield and Tennessee River Railway and pushed it on to the place that took his name, reached in 1889. It carried passengers from early on: the Mountain Eagle reported a southbound passenger train -- locomotive, tender, baggage car and coaches -- derailed two miles north of Blackwater in May 1889. Renamed the Northern Alabama Railway in 1899. Frequency estimated/unsourced.

The first 2.9 mi, Tuscumbia to Norala Junction, are main-line trackage shared with the Memphis and Charleston features above, so that stretch is drawn twice in this layer -- correctly, since the Parrish trains ran into Tuscumbia over it. LATER ALIGNMENT for that shared stretch, for the 1916 reason given above. The line continued south of Parrish to a Georgia Pacific connection west of Birmingham; that extension is not drawn.

segments.note: Renamed the Northern Alabama Railway in 1899 and worked under Southern Railway control; 105.748 mi of single-track standard-gauge road in two sections, of which Sheffield to Parrish was 94.876 mi. THE HEADWAY HERE IS THE ONE SOURCED NUMBER IN THIS LAYER'S FREQUENCIES, and it is a count of all traffic, not of this company's trains: in 1936 seven passenger trains ran daily through Lynn -- station 62, meaning 62 miles from Sheffield -- of which two were Northern Alabama, four Illinois Central and one Mobile and Ohio. Seven trains spread over a working day is roughly a five-hour headway; the Northern Alabama's own two would be twelve. Absorbed into the Southern Railway in 1939.

properties.geometry_source: Approximated on the present-day street grid from OpenStreetMap (ODbL) via Overpass, downtown Tuscumbia to downtown Sheffield to downtown Florence, crossing the Tennessee River on the traced Old Railroad Bridge alignment used by mc-sheffield-florence.
properties.geometry_quality: APPROXIMATE, 48 points, 7.4 mi. Only the river crossing is properly sourced geometry: the cars are documented to have run to Florence over the railroad portion of the Tennessee River bridge, and that 2.7 km is the traced rail alignment. The other 5.7 mi -- Tuscumbia to Sheffield, Sheffield out to the bridge, and the bridge into downtown Florence -- are shortest-path routes over today's streets between the three downtowns. NO SOURCE NAMING THE STREETS THE CARS ACTUALLY USED HAS BEEN CONSULTED, and no route mileage is documented to check the drawn length against. Treat the shape of this feature as a placeholder for a line that certainly existed on roughly this corridor, not as a traced route.

segments.note: The electric railway that tied the three Shoals cities together, and the reason the Southern's Sheffield-Florence local trains stopped in 1904. The Sheffield Company was founded that year to supply water and electricity to Sheffield, Florence and Tuscumbia, and ran a streetcar line between them. The Sheffield-Florence electric car line opened Jun 18 1904; in July 1904 the first car crossed to Florence over the railroad portion of the Tennessee River bridge, 'and thereafter hourly service was established' -- so the 60-minute headway on this segment is SOURCED, not estimated, unusually for this repository. Tagged interurban, not streetcar, under Rule 7: Florence, Sheffield and Tuscumbia were three separate incorporated cities and the line was built to join them, crossing a major river to do it. An earlier steam dummy line ran under the Sheffield Street Railway Company from 1891 to 1895; whether it followed this route is not sourced, so it is not drawn. Passed to Alabama Power in 1924.

segments.note: Alabama Power took the streetcars over from the Sheffield Company in 1924 and ran them for nine more years. THE END IS SOURCED TO THE HOUR: the last car crossed at midnight on Feb 3 1933, after which buses -- Burns Transportation Company, then Shoals Transit from 1941 -- replaced them. The headway is carried over from the hourly service established in 1904 and is not separately sourced for the Alabama Power years.
